source.author: cic
source.text: Cuius est vel maxime insigne illud exemplum, ut ceteras artis omittamus, quod dicebat Isocrates doctor singularis se calcaribus in Ephoro, contra autem in Theopompo frenis uti solere: alterum enim exsultantem verborum audacia reprimebat alterum cunctantem et quasi verecundantem incitabat.
source.text_original: Cuius est vel maxime insigne illud exemplum, ut ceteras artis omittamus, quod dicebat Isocrates doctor singularis se calcaribus in Ephoro, contra autem in Theopompo frenis uti solere: alterum enim exsultantem verborum audacia reprimebat alterum cunctantem et quasi verecundantem incitabat.
source.text_english: Of this kind the most notable example is that, to pass over the other arts, Isocrates, a teacher without peer, used to say that he was accustomed to use spurs on Ephorus, but reins on Theopompus; for with the one he checked the boldness of his words when it was overfree, while the other, who was hesitant and as it were shy, he urged on.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: Audio religiosam habere te matrem, multorum annorum uiduam, quae aluit, quae erudiuit infantem et post studia Galliarum, quae uel florentissima sunt, misit Romam non parcens sumptibus et absentiam filii spe sustinens futurorum, ut ubertatem Gallici nitoremque sermonis grauitas Romana condiret nec calcaribus in te sed frenis uteretur, quod et in disertissimis uiris Graeciae legimus, qui Asianum tumorem Attico siccabant sale et luxuriantes flagellis uineas falcibus reprimebant, ut eloquentiae torcularia non uerborum pampinis, sed sensuum quasi uuarum expressionibus redundarent.
reuse.text_original: Audio religiosam habere te matrem, multorum annorum uiduam, quae aluit, quae erudiuit infantem et post studia Galliarum, quae uel florentissima sunt, misit Romam non parcens sumptibus et absentiam filii spe sustinens futurorum, ut ubertatem Gallici nitoremque sermonis grauitas Romana condiret nec calcaribus in te sed frenis uteretur, quod et in disertissimis uiris Graeciae legimus, qui Asianum tumorem Attico siccabant sale et luxuriantes flagellis uineas falcibus reprimebant, ut eloquentiae torcularia non uerborum pampinis, sed sensuum quasi uuarum expressionibus redundarent.
reuse.text_english: I hear that you have a devout mother, a widow of many years, who nourished you and educated you as an infant, and after your studies in Gaul, which are among the most flourishing, sent you to Rome, sparing no expense and bearing her son’s absence in hope of future things, so that the Roman seriousness might temper the richness and brilliance of Gallic speech, and that she would use not spurs on you but reins. This too we read in the most eloquent men of Greece, who would dry up Asian bombast with Attic salt and restrain luxuriant vines with pruning hooks, so that the wine-presses of eloquence might overflow not with clusters of words, but, as it were, with the pressing out of thoughts like grapes.
